The demand for alligator products is only latent. There are several species of endangered carnivores which produce furs that have had special value to man. Mollusks include a number of species or subspecies commercially valuable for their shells.
Sport uses include hunting, fishing, and falconry and are a generator of economic return through sale of associated equipment and services. Of 179 species and subspecies included in the "Red Book," approximately 40 have a past history of sporting use as well as a potential for redevelopment of that use if restoration is sufficiently successful. Most of this group are fishes.
Power and energy production represent an important resource to the United States. Development of those resources can affect endangered species and subspecies through inundation of habitat and the alteration of water quality. Timber harvest and forestry practices represent a use of the land resource that can be in competition with endangered species. Adverse effects occur through removal of forest habitats, the stream siltation that occurs from erosion that follows cutting, and the effects of modern forestry practices such as suppression of natural fire and removal of over-aged, diseased, and dying trees. Mining and oil drilling disrupt the welfare of an endangered species through pollution or disturbance and removal of habitat.
Probably the broadest economic interest affecting endangered species is that connected with livestock production and agricultural crops. Fifty-seven species and subspecies in the "Red Book" will likely bring about an increase in the cost of such livestock or agricultural resources if the endangered species is successfully restored.
